title: Order API timeouts overnight
executive_summary: INC-004: Order creation latency and timeouts began at 02:15Z. Earlier signals show the sequence: the invoice-reconciliation batch job started at 02:05Z on order-7f9c; CPU rose at 02:08Z; GC pauses of 2.6-9.7 s started at 02:08Z; memory rose from 02:10Z; the order-worker pool saturated at 02:12Z; p50 latency rose at 02:13Z; and error and timeout rates rose at 02:15Z. No deployments or config changes were recorded. Request rate was flat. Database connection utilisation was flat. Postgres CPU rose modestly (about 24%) from 02:11Z, likely a secondary effect. Status is PROBABLE because per-node and batch-job metrics are unavailable.

hypotheses.description: Invoice-reconciliation batch job (batch_size=500000) started on an order-service node at 02:05Z and saturated CPU and heap, causing GC thrash and thread-pool exhaustion. Mechanism: The batch job consumes CPU and allocates heavily on a serving node; G1 evacuation pauses of 7-10 s stall request threads; the order-worker pool fills (active=200, queue ~19k); requests exceed the 5000 ms deadline.

root_cause_statement: MOST PROBABLE EXPLANATION (INFERENCE, not confirmed): resource_saturation in order-service - Invoice-reconciliation batch job (batch_size=500000) started on an order-service node at 02:05Z and saturated CPU and heap, causing GC thrash and thread-pool exhaustion.
corrective_actions: Stop or throttle the invoice-reconciliation job on order-7f9c (reduce batch_size) to relieve CPU and GC pressure
Restart or drain order-service pods showing GC thrash to restore worker threads
Move the reconciliation job to dedicated batch workers
preventive_actions: Isolate batch and scheduled jobs from request-serving nodes
Add batch_size limits and CPU and heap guardrails to scheduled jobs
Add a runbook step to check scheduled jobs at the start of overnight incidents
monitoring_recommendations: Alert on per-node CPU above 85% and GC pause above 1 s for order-service
Alert on order-worker queue depth and thread-pool saturation
Track the batch job's runtime, CPU and heap usage
Collect per-node metrics for all order-service nodes; disk_io_wait is currently not collected
limitations: Timing correlation with the batch job start does not prove causation
Aggregate metrics may hide a single hot node
Historical match is only an analogy

Confidence values are rule-based evidence-strength scores, not calibrated probabilities.
conclusion: Order-service overnight timeouts were most likely caused by resource saturation on order-service nodes (CPU and heap/GC thrash) that began about 02:08Z, shortly after the scheduled invoice-reconciliation batch job (batch_size=500000) started on node order-7f9c at 02:05Z. The saturation exhausted the order-worker thread pool, producing deadline-exceeded timeouts. No deployment or configuration change was recorded. The causal link to the batch job is inferred from timing and a historical analogy; the job's own resource usage is not directly measured.
